## Task given to both responders

Explain what a database index is and why adding one can make writes slower.

## Response A

A database index is a secondary data structure the database maintains alongside a table to speed up lookups. The most common form is a B-tree: the indexed column's values are kept in sorted order, each pointing to the location of the corresponding row. Without an index, answering `WHERE email = 'x'` means scanning every row in the table. With one, the database walks a few levels of the tree and jumps straight to the matches.

The catch is that an index is redundant, derived data, and redundant data must be kept in sync. Every INSERT writes the row and then adds an entry to each index on that table. Every DELETE removes both. An UPDATE touching an indexed column is effectively a delete plus an insert in that index, even though the row itself hasn't moved. A table with five indexes can therefore do six writes' worth of work per row change.

There are second-order costs too. Index pages stay sorted, so inserting into a full page causes a page split — extra I/O and fragmentation. Random keys like UUIDs scatter writes across the whole index, hurting cache locality. Indexes also enlarge the write-ahead log and add latch contention on hot pages.

That's the trade: cheaper reads, and a write tax roughly proportional to how many indexes you keep.

## Response B

An index is a separate, sorted data structure — usually a B-tree — that maps column values to row locations, so the database can jump straight to matching rows instead of scanning the whole table. Writes get slower because every insert, update, or delete must also update each index: extra I/O, page splits, and locking on top of the table write itself.

## Task given to both responders

Explain what a database index is and why adding one can make writes slower.

## Response A

A database index is an auxiliary data structure — typically a B-tree or similar sorted structure — built on one or more columns of a table to speed up data retrieval. Instead of scanning every row to find matches (a full table scan), the database engine can use the index to jump almost directly to the relevant rows, similar to how a book's index lets you find a topic without reading every page. This dramatically speeds up SELECT queries, especially on large tables, and it's also used to enforce uniqueness constraints and speed up JOIN operations.

The tradeoff appears on writes. Every time you INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE a row, the database doesn't just modify the underlying table data — it must also update every index that covers the affected columns, to keep them consistent with the table. If a table has five indexes, a single insert becomes six write operations: one for the table's data pages, and five for the index structures. Each of those index updates may involve rebalancing a tree, writing to additional disk pages, and taking additional locks, which increases I/O and can create contention when multiple writes happen concurrently.

This is why indexing is a tradeoff: it speeds up reads at the cost of write throughput and storage. In practice, teams index columns that are frequently searched, while avoiding excessive indexes on write-heavy tables, since each one compounds the penalty.

## Response B

A database index is a separate data structure (often a B-tree) that stores sorted references to rows, letting queries find matching rows quickly instead of scanning the whole table. Writes get slower because every insert, update, or delete must also update each index: more data structures to maintain per write, plus extra disk I/O and lock contention, especially with many indexes.

## Task given to both responders

Explain what a database index is and why adding one can make writes slower.

## Response A

A database index is a specialized data structure, typically a B-tree or hash table, that enables the database to quickly locate rows without scanning the entire table. When you index a column, the database creates a separate sorted structure pointing back to the original rows. For queries, this is enormously efficient—instead of checking millions of rows, the database can use the index to find matching records in logarithmic time.

However, this comes at a cost for write operations. When you insert, update, or delete a row, the database must maintain not just the main table but every index on that table. Each index needs to be updated to reflect the change, which takes additional I/O operations and computational resources. A table with five indexes requires roughly five times the write work of an unindexed table.

The slowdown becomes particularly noticeable during bulk operations like large imports or batch updates. Moreover, indexes consume disk space, which has implications for caching efficiency and backup times.

This trade-off is why database design requires careful planning: you index columns frequently used in WHERE clauses and joins, but avoid over-indexing write-heavy tables. The goal is to balance query performance against write latency and storage costs.

## Response B

A database index is a data structure (like a B-tree) that speeds up data retrieval by pre-sorting columns. Instead of scanning every row, queries can jump directly to relevant data. However, indexes slow writes because the database must update both the table and all its indexes. More indexes mean more write overhead, creating a trade-off between read speed and write performance.

## Task given to both responders

Explain idempotency to a product manager with no distributed systems background, in a way that helps them reason about what to promise customers. No bullet points, no headings.

## Response A

Idempotency is the property that doing the same operation twice leaves the system in the same state as doing it once. Pressing a lift button five times doesn't summon five lifts. Charging a card is the opposite: do it twice and the customer is out twice the money.

It matters because of one specific way networks fail. When a client sends a request and gets no answer back, it cannot tell whether the request never arrived or whether it succeeded and the reply was lost on the way home. The only safe move is to retry, and retries are where duplicates come from. Idempotency is what makes retrying safe.

The usual mechanism is an idempotency key: the client attaches a unique identifier to each intended action, and if the server sees that key again it returns the original result rather than doing the work a second time.

For customer promises, this means you can commit to something like "a retried payment will not create a second charge," as long as the client sends a key and the retry arrives inside the server's retention window, often 24 hours. You cannot promise that every message is delivered exactly once — nobody can. What you can promise is exactly-once effects built on top of at-least-once delivery. And be clear that this protects against repeats of the same request, not against two genuinely different requests that happen to look similar.

## Response B

Idempotency means doing the same operation twice has the same effect as doing it once. Networks drop responses, so clients retry, and without idempotency a retry can charge a customer twice. You can promise "we won't double-charge" only if requests carry a client-supplied key the server remembers, and only for the window it retains those keys. Promise exactly-once effects, never exactly-once delivery.

## Task given to both responders

Explain idempotency to a product manager with no distributed systems background, in a way that helps them reason about what to promise customers. No bullet points, no headings.

## Response A

Idempotency is the property that lets you do the same thing twice without it happening twice. Imagine a customer taps 'submit payment' and the app seems to freeze, so they tap it again. Without idempotency, that second tap can trigger a second charge, because the system just processes each request as a brand new instruction. With idempotency, the system recognizes that this is the same request as before, perhaps because it carries a unique identifier the client generated, and it responds as if it already did the work, without doing it again. The customer sees one charge, one order, one email, no matter how many times the request was retried. This matters commercially because networks are unreliable: requests time out, connections drop, and mobile apps retry automatically. If your systems aren't idempotent, every one of those routine hiccups risks a duplicate charge, a duplicate shipment, or a duplicate notification, and support has to clean it up manually. When you're deciding what to promise customers, ask your engineers whether a given action, like charging a card or placing an order, is idempotent. If it is, you can safely tell customers that retrying or refreshing is safe and won't cause double charges. If it isn't, you should either avoid exposing a retry button to users, or explicitly caveat that duplicate submissions might cause duplicate effects until the underlying action is made idempotent.

## Response B

Idempotency means doing the same operation twice has the same effect as doing it once. If a customer resubmits a payment request after a network hiccup, an idempotent system won't charge them twice. You can promise customers that retries are safe and won't cause duplicate charges or duplicate orders, but only for actions your team has explicitly designed to be idempotent.

## Task given to both responders

Explain idempotency to a product manager with no distributed systems background, in a way that helps them reason about what to promise customers. No bullet points, no headings.

## Response A

Idempotency is a property where repeating an operation produces the same outcome as doing it once. Think of a light switch: flipping it on ten times leaves the light in the same state as flipping it on once. That predictability is what idempotency delivers.

In distributed systems, networks fail. A customer clicks "submit payment," but their connection drops—they don't know if it went through, so they click again. Without idempotency, both requests hit your system, and they're charged twice. With it, the second request gets caught and safely ignored because you recognize it as a duplicate.

From a product perspective, idempotency is about building trust. Customers can retry without fear. They can instruct other systems to retry automatically. Your service becomes dependable in the face of real-world unreliability.

The tradeoff is that idempotency requires you to track which operations you've already processed—via request IDs, transaction deduplication, or similar mechanisms. This adds storage and computation.

But the benefit is enormous: you can promise customers that critical operations won't mysteriously duplicate. A transfer of funds always transfers exactly once, no matter how many retries happen underneath. That kind of safety is what transforms unreliable networks into systems people can actually trust with their business.

## Response B

Idempotency means an operation produces the same result regardless of how many times you execute it. Think of it like pressing an elevator button: pressing once or ten times still takes you to the same floor. For customers, this is crucial: if a payment request is accidentally sent twice, idempotency ensures they're only charged once. It's a reliability promise that makes systems predictable and safe.
